abstract: Estrogen receptor beta (ER{beta}) is a ligand-activated nuclear steroid receptor that promotes neuroprotection through its transcriptional coordination of healthy cell gene programs. However, circulating estrogens are dramatically reduced post-menopause and the administration of hormone replacement therapy is only beneficial within a narrowly restricted timeframe after the menopause transition. The molecular underpinnings for this failure of ER{beta} to evoke protection in advanced age is unknown. Evidence suggests that age-related changes in protein-protein interactions could preclude ER{beta} genomic signaling. Protein-protein interactions can be regulated and modified through post-translational modifications (PTM)s of individual amino acid residues; the most well-studied PTM being phosphorylation. Our prior work showed that ER{beta} phosphorylation was age-dependent leading to the hypothesis that ER{beta} phosphorylation is required for ER{beta}-protein interactions, specifically ER{beta} homodimer formation. We used fluorescence lifetime measurements to quantify Forster resonance energy transfer (FRET) of ER{beta}-S176, S200, and Y488 phosphomutant protein interactions. Overall, our results demonstrate that phosphorylation of ER{beta}-S176, S200, and Y488 reduced ER{beta} homodimer formation, suggesting an age-dependent molecular mechanism that regulates ER{beta} genomic signaling. Moreover, phosphorylation at S200 and Y488 resulted in a loss of ER{beta}-mediated amyloid precursor protein (APP) promoter gene repression providing evidence that these age-dependent PTMs directly impact ER{beta}'s function as a transcription factor. Taken together, these data suggest that age-dependent changes in ER{beta} phosphorylation result in decreased ER{beta} genomic signaling, which could reduce the neuroprotective effects of estrogens following menopause.
